name: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA peel)

lead: TCA is a strong acid used as a medium-depth chemical peel. Clinicians use it for smoother texture, less uneven pigment and some acne scars, with visible skin renewal after healing.

The acid causes controlled chemical injury to the skin surface, which then peels and regenerates, and the depth depends on concentration and technique. Small trials are registered for acne, melasma, lentigines and scars, but the registry entries cited do not report results.

paras: It is a provider-performed procedure in a clinic or outpatient setting. A warm or burning sensation is common, and the skin peels over the following days before new skin shows.

The European Chemicals Agency says the acid causes severe skin burns and eye damage. Deeper peels carry risks of prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, atrophy and scarring, and Wikipedia says medium peels should be done by a medical provider.

chain: New skin forms in its place
Smoother texture, less pigment and scarring
angle.text: A TCA peel removes damaged outer skin so new skin forms in its place, leaving smoother texture and less pigment and scarring. Clinicians perform it, and the visible renewal shows after healing.

lead: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is a strong organic acid used in dermatology as a chemical peel and as a topical agent to destroy warts. It was discovered by the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839, and in laboratories is widely used to precipitate proteins and nucleic acids.[1]

A TCA peel is classed as a medium-depth peel, which Wikipedia says should be performed by a medical provider, usually in a clinic or outpatient surgical setting; patients commonly report a warm or burning sensation.[2] General complications of deeper peels include prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, atrophy and scarring.[2]

Registered studies include TCA peels for acne, melasma, lentigines and atrophic varicella scars; the registry records cited here do not report outcomes.[3][4][5][6] A point-wise variant known as TCA CROSS is used by clinicians for atrophic scars, but none of the sources cited here describe it.
infobox: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage (ECHA)[1]

paras: TCA is applied to the skin to cause controlled chemical injury, followed by peeling and regrowth. It is regarded as a medium peel, with deeper effects than light superficial acids.[2] Concentration, number of coats and technique influence depth; specific protocols are the province of treating clinicians and are not given here.

Registered studies have examined TCA for acne vulgaris, melasma, hand lentigines, atrophic varicella scars and acanthosis nigricans.[3][4][5][6][7] Cosmetic uses of TCA also include chemical peels and tattoo removal.[1]
TCA is applied topically to destroy warts, including genital warts, and has been registered in studies for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.[1][8]

The European Chemicals Agency classifies TCA as causing severe skin burns and eye damage.[1] Wikipedia lists photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigmentary changes, milia, atrophy and textural change among the complications of deeper peels, and notes injury and scarring from professional and home peels.[2] The IARC lists TCA in Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), which concerns chemical exposure generally.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a 2022 trial of 25% TCA peel versus 30% salicylic acid peel in mild to moderate acne (n=60)[3], a trial of TCA for atrophic varicella scars (n=100)[4], a melasma trial of modified Jessner's solution with TCA versus glycolic acid with TCA (n=30)[5], a 15% TCA peel for hand lentigines (n=20)[6] and a trial comparing 15% TCA with tretinoin in acanthosis nigricans (n=80).[7] The registry records cited here do not report results, so outcomes are not summarized.
No community sources are cited for this entry. TCA peels and TCA CROSS are discussed as clinic procedures in acne-scar and skin-texture conversations.
